items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall that an exponential expression such as [MATH: x^{1/2}] can be written as [MATH: \sqrt x,] the square root of [MATH: x.]

Content:
Similarly [MATH: z^{1/3}] can be written as [MATH: \sqrt[3]{z},] the cube root of [MATH: z.]

Content:
In general, the fractional exponent [MATH: x^{1/n}] can be written as the [MATH: n]th root [MATH: \sqrt[n]{x}.]

Content:
So, how might we rewrite the following exponential expression as a radical?

Content:
[MATH: y^{4/7}]
Notice that the exponent is a non-unit fraction because the numerator [MATH: (4)] does not equal [MATH: 1.]

Content:
To rewrite [MATH: y^{4/7}] as a radical, we use the rules of exponents.

Content:
First, using the power law for exponents, we can write our expression as
[MATH: y^{4/7} = \left(y^4\right)^{1/7}.]

Content:
Notice that we now have an expression [MATH: (y^4)] raised to a unit fraction [MATH: (1/7).] So, we can write our expression as
[MATH: \left(y^4\right)^{1/7} = \sqrt[7]{y^4}.]

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that
[MATH: y^{4/7} = \sqrt[7]{y^4}.]

Content:

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, using the power law for exponents, we can write our expression as [MATH: \left(6n\right)^{2/3} = \left((6n)^2\right)^{1/3}.]

In general, the fractional exponent [MATH: x^{1/n}] can also be written as the [MATH: n]th root [MATH: \sqrt[n]{x}.]

In this particular case, [MATH: n=3] and [MATH: x=(6n)^2.] Therefore, we have [MATH: \left((6n)^2\right)^{1/3} = \sqrt[3]{(6n)^2} = \sqrt[3]{36\,n^2}.]

sections.readable_text: Write [MATH: \sqrt[11]{\left(\dfrac{5}{a}\right)^{2}}] using a fractional exponent.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:

In this particular case, [MATH: n=11] and [MATH: x=\left(\dfrac{5}{a}\right)^2.] Therefore, we have [MATH: \sqrt[11]{\left(\dfrac{5}{a}\right)^{2}}=\left(\left(\dfrac{5}{a}\right)^{2}\right)^{1/11}.]

items.title: Converting a Negative Fractional Exponent to a Radical

sections.normalized_html: Convert [MATH: (8y)^{-3/2}] into a radical.
sections.readable_text: Convert [MATH: (8y)^{-3/2}] into a radical.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Remember that in general, a negative exponent can be converted to a positive exponent if we take the reciprocal. Here, we have

[MATH: (8y)^{-3/2} = \dfrac{1}{(8y)^{3/2}}.]

Next, using the power law for exponents, we can write our expression as

[MATH: \dfrac{1}{(8y)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{1}{\left((8y)^3\right)^{1/2}}.]

Now, we can proceed as usual to convert the fractional exponent to a radical:

[MATH: \dfrac{1}{\left((8y)^3\right)^{1/2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{(8y)^3}}]

Therefore, we have

[MATH: (8y)^{-3/2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{(8y)^3}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{512y^3}}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In general, the fractional exponent [MATH: x^{1/n}] can be written as the [MATH: n]th root [MATH: \sqrt[n]{x}.]

Content:
So, how might we rewrite the following exponential expression as a radical?

Content:
[MATH: y^{4/7}]
Notice that the exponent is a non-unit fraction because the numerator [MATH: (4)] does not equal [MATH: 1.]

Content:
To rewrite [MATH: y^{4/7}] as a radical, we use the rules of exponents.

Content:
First, using the power law for exponents, we can write our expression as
[MATH: y^{4/7} = \left(y^4\right)^{1/7}.]

Content:
Notice that we now have an expression [MATH: (y^4)] raised to a unit fraction [MATH: (1/7).] So, we can write our expression as
[MATH: \left(y^4\right)^{1/7} = \sqrt[7]{y^4}.]

[MATH: y^{4/7} = \sqrt[7]{y^4}.]
